title: High-Skill AI Wage Premium
description: Measured pay advantage for workers with AI/ML skills over comparable workers without them. Unlike most graphs on this site, every estimate here is an observation of a premium that already exists — none of them is a forecast.
disclaimer: The estimates here run from 3% to 62%, and the gap is mostly about what gets measured. The high numbers come from job advertisements: what employers offer for roles that ask for AI skills. The low numbers come from workers' actual paychecks. Advertised pay runs ahead of realized pay because the roles asking for AI skills are also more senior, more urban, and concentrated in industries that paid well already — so a posting premium credits AI for a gap that is partly seniority and location. Read the postings figures as the price of the job and the worker-level figures as the return to the skill. Because these studies bracket different quantities rather than track one over time, the graph shows no trend line.

sources.title: Complement or Substitute? How AI Increases the Demand for Human Skills

sources.title: Generative AI in Daily Business Practice: Synthesis of Micro-Level Firm Evidence
sources.publisher: Maastricht University (Fregin, Eijkenboom, Özgül-Persyn, Pardesi, Rounding — DOI 10.26481/umarpb.2026002e)
sources.excerpt: Synthesis of micro-level firm evidence finds generative AI already embedded in everyday business practice. Productivity gains in the near term come from task reallocation and upskilling rather than headcount reduction, with high-skill workers who effectively augment their output capturing a widening wage premium. The brief cautions that this benign short-run picture may mask longer-run structural displacement.

Compensation growth in technology and professional services has cooled as hiring normalizes.

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Skill Premium
sources.excerpt: We show that AI reduces the skill premium as long as it is more substitutable for high-skill workers than low-skill workers are for high-skill workers. [...] This leads to a skill premium of about 2, i.e., wages of high-skill workers are twice the wages of low-skill workers. In the second row, G_t is half the value of P_t and the skill premium decreases to about 1.7. In the third row, the value of G_t is now the same as the value of P_t so that the skill premium shrinks further to 1.62.

sources.title: AI Adoption and Inequality (IMF Working Paper 2025/068)
sources.excerpt: Under the baseline assumption that occupational exposure to AI is directly associated with task displacement, the model predicts a decrease in the Gini coefficient for wage inequality of 1.73 p.p. Wealth inequality, however, is predicted to widen, with the wealth Gini rising 7.18 p.p. [...] roughly 60 percent of workers at the 90th income percentile are in an occupation where a large share of tasks can be performed by AI, at the 10th percentile only 15 percent of workers are in this situation. For comparison, the model calibrated to routine-biased automation produces a substantial increase in both wage and wealth inequality, with the Gini rising by 2.05 p.p. and 6.89 p.p., respectively.

sources.title: Agentic coding and persistent returns to expertise
sources.publisher: Anthropic Economic Research (Hitzig, Massenkoff, Lyubich, Zhang, Heller, McCrory)
sources.excerpt: Anthropic Economic Research (Hitzig, Massenkoff, Lyubich, Zhang, Heller, McCrory — Jun 16, 2026). Analysis of ~400,000 Claude Code sessions from ~235,000 users between Oct 2025 and Apr 2026. Verified success rates: 'Novice: 15%; Intermediate/Expert: 28-33%.' Partial success rates: 77% (novice) vs 91-92% (intermediate/expert). Abandonment when troubled: novice 19% vs intermediate+ 5-7%. 'Every one of the ten largest occupations in our dataset lands within seven points of software engineers' (29-34% verified success). 'The estimated value of the average session rose by 27% between October and April.' Division of labor: 'people make about 70% of the planning decisions but only 20% of the execution decisions.' Work mix: code writing/fixing/testing 56%, ops 17%, planning/exploration 14%, analysis/prose 13%. Novice: ~5 actions, 600 words output/prompt; Expert: ~12 actions, 3,200 words/prompt.

sources.title: PwC 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer
sources.excerpt: PwC 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer (Atkinson & Brown, Jun 15, 2026). Analyzed 1+ billion job advertisements across 27 countries and territories, including 2.4M entry-level US jobs. Key findings: entry-level roles most exposed to AI are 'seven times more likely to require traditionally senior-level skills'; job openings for 'seniorised' entry-level roles grew 35% since 2019 while other entry-level roles declined 10%. AI-skills wage premium reached 62% (up from 57% in the 2025 barometer), ranging from 16% (government) to 118% (consumer markets). AI-skill jobs growing 69% vs 9% for the total jobs market — 'almost twice as high as 2024.' Companies most exposed to AI: 52% headcount growth vs 36% (least exposed); wage growth 24% vs 17%; productivity 34% vs 24% (2018-2025), with the top-20% 'super-stars' at 163% productivity gain. 'Professionalised' roles growing twice as fast with 42% faster salary increases. Technology/media/telecom: 11% AI job share; health: <1%.

sources.title: Google's AI & Economy ATLAS v1.0: Mapping Gemini Usage in the Economy
sources.publisher: Google / Google DeepMind (Iscenko, Strand, Imas, Manyika et al.)
sources.excerpt: Google's AI & Economy ATLAS v1.0 (Iscenko, Strand, Chen, Imas, Manyika et al., Google/Google DeepMind, Jul 23 2026; reviewed by Diane Coyle and David Autor). 15M de-identified interactions across Gemini App, AI Mode, and Gemini API (Apr 6-19, 2026), mapped to 800+ occupations, 4,000 O*NET tasks, 300 ATUS activities, 150 countries, 140 languages. Work: 'AI adoption spans occupations covering just above 88% of US employment' (68% of detailed occupations) but 'penetration remains shallow' — 'AI is used for only 21% of total tasks in the median occupation with any AI use'; only 3% of occupations show usage for >75% of tasks. 'Attempts to automate tasks end-to-end represent less than 10% of AI conversations in non-routine cognitive work'; >25% for routine cognitive work. Non-routine cognitive tasks = 35% of O*NET universe but 65% of work interactions. Wages: 'a 1% increase in an occupation's median earnings is associated with a more than 2.5% increase in AI usage intensity'; Gemini-weighted median salary $82,919 vs $62,252 employment-weighted national median. Home: 86% of conversational use is non-work; government/civic queries over-represented ~20x vs time spent; household time-savings valued at $14.9B-$149B/yr (0.5-5% scenarios). Global: 1% GDP/capita ↑ → 0.9% usage ↑; English only ~1/3 of conversations across 143 languages.

sources.title: AI Labor Market Tracker: July 2026
sources.excerpt: The wage premium for AI-exposed work has eroded to roughly zero, falling from around 2% before ChatGPT's launch. Measured as the salary premium associated with a one-standard-deviation increase in posting-level AI exposure, not as a premium over the median wage.

sources.title: Are AI Certifications Worth It? What the Salary Data Shows
sources.excerpt: Revelio Labs analysis of AI certifications recorded on workers' online professional profiles, built from a two-level taxonomy of over 500,000 unique AI-related certification names. "After controlling for occupation and seniority level, AI certification holders earn, on average, an $8,000 salary premium compared to non-certification holders." Revelio frames this as positive selection rather than a return to certification: "within any given occupation and seniority level, the workers choosing to get certifications are those who are already earning more than their peers." Certification share rose from 1-2% of all professional certifications pre-ChatGPT to nearly 30% by 2026, a 20x increase. A propensity-score-matched comparison finds certification takers see salary grow 18.1% in their next position versus 15.3% for non-takers.

sources.title: The Impact of AI on the U.S. Labor Market: Early Evidence from Observed Adoption
sources.excerpt: Management and professional occupations also had significant impacts on their real wage growth, as it fell 4.1% relative to non-exposure peers. Blue-collar workers showed no statistically significant effects. Measures a growth differential versus non-exposed occupations, not a premium over the median wage.

sources.title: The Wage Effects of Generative AI
sources.excerpt: Workers who report GenAI-related skills receive a conditional starting-wage premium of approximately 8-9 percent. At the same time, the coefficient on the cell-level GenAI worker share is -0.151 when entered without predetermined exposure and -0.122 when both measures are included. There is no contradiction between these findings. A worker who reports GenAI-related skills may command a premium relative to otherwise comparable workers, while starting wages decline in cells where those skills become more prevalent. The authors treat these skill-based exercises as descriptive conditional associations, not causal returns to acquiring GenAI skills, because reported skills may respond to wages and worker composition.
